svg.title: Why compression tools save only 1 to 3 percent of the bill, and what they cost you
svg.desc: Share of Claude Code cost in 456 bkit transcripts: 69 percent is the model re-reading the system prompt, rules, tool list and conversation; 4 percent is the model's own writing; 27 percent is big tool output, the only part a compressor can touch; the tools remove 1 to 3 percent of the bill. Gains: 1 to 3 percent saved, big cuts on huge logs, prompt cache intact. Costs: wrong answers, broken code, hidden content, silent failures, a proxy that sees all model traffic, clashes with bkit's setup.
svg.text: Why compression tools save only 1–3% of the bill
Where Claude Code's cost goes, across 456 real bkit transcripts (the whole bar is 100% of the bill)
69% The model re-reading everything else
system prompt, rules, tool list, and the conversation so far, on every request
27% Big tool output
the only part a compressor can touch (orange included)
4% The model's own writing
1–3% What the tools actually remove
The tools that remove more get there by cutting code and logs the agent needs to read exactly.
So is it worth it? A modest saving, real risks
What you gain
What it costs you: cons and risks
Saves 1–3% of the bill
on typical bkit work
Big cuts on huge logs and git history
up to 95% on one 1.2 MB git log
Prompt cache stays intact
so nothing else gets more expensive
Wrong answers.
An agent answered a question wrongly from a compressed
log and never fetched the original.
Broken code.
Kompress turned “=> void” into “void”; RTK strips indentation and
cuts lines at 80 characters, so edits quoting them fail.
Hidden content.
Cut text comes back only if the agent notices the marker and
asks, and asking costs tokens, which eats into the saving.
Silent failures.
A missing dependency or an ignored setting switches compression
off with no warning: seen with caveman and Headroom, and RTK's
hook is built to do the same.
A proxy sees all your model traffic.
A supply-chain and security risk; the
caveman release tested was one day old.
Clashes with bkit's own setup.
A tool added to every agent (caveman), a second permission
decision beside bkit's gates (RTK), edits to global settings.
Source: tests/compression/bkit-caveman-headroom-compression-proxy-comparison.md (T3, T4, T5, T7)
